title: Evaluation of the resorption kinetics and the ethanol degradation per hour in blood
summary:
A decision by the Federal Court of Justice (BGH) on 11 December 1973 set the cornerstones of our current recalculation of a measured blood alcohol concentration to the time of an incident. A previously staggered recalculation for the minimum reduction, which provided for values between 0.10 and 0.12 ‰/h (0.10 ‰ in the first hour after the end of drinking, 0.12 ‰/h from the second hour onwards), was reduced to a statistically proven minimum value of 0.10 ‰/h. In the corresponding publication in the Neue Juristische Wochenschrift from 1974, the then senior public prosecutor Konrad Händel also discussed the resorption phase [1]. The underlying scientific data dates back to the 1960s and 1970s. In 1976, Zink and Reinhardt dealt with the topic of back-calculation to maximum blood alcohol concentrations [2] and analysed 1486 alcohol curves. In a publication by Gerchow et al., the hourly degradation rate is given as a weighted average of 4233 individual values at 0.148 ‰/h [3]. However, the large database in both publications is limited due to inhomogeneous primary data collection. The different design of the studies and differing measurement methods limit the informative value. 
From a scientific point of view, the question arises as to the extent to which the reduction rates determined in this way for retroactive calculation can still be reliably applied almost 50 years after the BGH decision. In order to answer this question, a standardised, multi-centre study with a blood alcohol determination according to forensic criteria for the most comprehensive data collection possible is recommended. 
Volunteers will be asked to abstain from alcohol for at least 2 days and to eat a light breakfast approximately 2 hours before the trial. Abstinence is checked by means of a so-called zero sample (blood alcohol) and beforehand by means of a breath alcohol test. To assess alcohol consumption behaviour, the concentration of the direct alcohol consumption marker phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is determined from the zero sample. It is planned to give the test subjects alcoholic drinks (vodka, possibly mixed with carbonated and non-alcoholic drinks) in a quantity that leads to a probable blood alcohol concentration of 1.0 ‰ calculated using the Widmark formula (taking into account the drinking time). If possible, the alcoholic beverages should be drunk within 90 minutes. The total amount is portioned and given to the test subjects in such a way that the alcohol intake is evenly distributed within the planned time period. 
Blood samples are taken 15 minutes before and after the end of drinking and at 30-minute intervals for 2.5 hours from the end of the drinking period. Thereafter, blood samples are taken at 60-minute intervals for up to 5 further hours until the end of the experiment (either peripheral venous access or single puncture) until sobering up is achieved. Serum is promptly obtained from the blood samples (‘Abseren’). At the same time, the breath alcohol concentration is measured as an orientation check for decreasing alcoholisation. Starting 4 hours after the start of drinking, the test persons can eat again (e.g. pizza, sandwiches).
conditions: Re-evaluation of the hourly ethanol degradation rate in healthy volunteers

interventions.name: healthy volunteers, drinking alcoholic beverages in a calculated amount, leading to a blood ethanol concentration of 1.0 g/kg. Thereafter, blood samples taken at 30-minute or 60-minute intervals to evaluate the rate of degradation of ethanol in blood.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- good health 
	- Previous alcohol consumption in comparable quantities without problems
	- Age ≥ 20 years
	- proficient in written and spoken German
	- Ability to consent
	- abstinence from alcohol for at least 2 days before the start of the trial
Exclusion criteria:
- Severe cardiovascular or respiratory diseases (requiring treatment) 
	- Liver or kidney disease
	- severe mental illnesses (requiring treatment) and/or
- severe neurological diseases
- Severe underlying illnesses (e.g. tumour diseases)
	- Addiction problems (AUDIT score ≥15)
	- Alcohol intolerance (e.g. flush syndrome after alcohol intake)
	- Diabetes mellitus
	- Poor state of health
	- Pregnancy and breastfeeding (pregnancy test for women < 50 years)
- Medication intake with interaction with ethanol degradation
- Persons unable to give consent
	- Poor vein conditions
